blocks.x: My name is Carl Rinker and I play trumpet. I played in Chicago from starting about 1924 until roughly about 1939 when I discontinued trumpet playing to go into other work.

During that time I played with many musicians from New Orleans. I believe the first one I met was Rag Baby Stevens, drummer. That was when I was playing out on Milwaukee Avenue about the first job I ever played. A place called the House of Niles. I think I met Larry Shields there also. Shortly after that I played at a place on West Madison Street owned by Tommy Thomas in which Ray Bozeman was the saxophone clarinet player and he was a very excellent one. And shortly after that I met the Bruny's boys Merritt, Henry, and George and later Paul Merez of course. I remembered them for many years and became quite friendly with Paul Merez later on. After that I played with Lester Bouchon and his friend Westerfield. We called him Eagle. I can't remember his first name. They were both saxophone players, excellent ones. I knew Steve Brown. I played with him at the Midway Gardens. Natty Dominick, a personal friend of mine at Burt Kelly Stables. He is to this day. He taught me much about the trumpet. And of course I know the boys that played with the uh with the Pollack and the uh and the Bobcat bands. Benny Pollack and later with the Bobcats there was uh Irving Pizzola. I knew him quite well. Played with him several times. And uh Matty Matlock, Nappy Lamar, Eddie Miller, and Ray Badouf whom I knew well. Let's see who else from New Orleans. Oh there were so many. Many of the colored musicians from New Orleans I knew. How many of them came from there and how many didn't I don't I really know. Let's see. I got to know Paul quite well when he was running his Shrimp de Jong place on uh Bryn Mawr and I was living close to there. He used to pick up his telephone and call me and then he would play the trumpet to me and I would play the trumpet back to him. And we used to pass the evenings away that way occasionally. That was not too long before he passed away. I don't know John if I can remember anybody else in New Orleans or not. So many fellas came from there that I didn't really know. Uh perhaps uh what was that trombone player's name again? Uh. Maxon. Roy Maxon I knew him and uh uh uh in uh uh uh

talking with uh Bill about his uh uh year, Carl really, in talking to Carl about his years in uh Chicago Jazz I discovered that he crossed lines frequently and so on the uh 16th of uh October 1962 I asked him to put down a few comments on tape on some of these uh people that he had mentioned as we went over the interview. Uh I thought that many of his comments about their playing quality was interesting. What did you think of uh Bouchon as a uh baritone player? I could say he was the greatest

saxophone and clarinet player I ever heard uh but who knows who is the greatest. I know he pleased me in every way and uh well he could have been uh uh he's certainly among the greatest. Westerfield you said it was also a saxophone. Very good. He played tenor saxophone and clarinet quite well. Uh Ray Bozeman uh was also very good. Les Bouchon was fine on clarinet and on uh baritone saxophone. These are all in the uh

in the 20s that you encountered these. In the 20s yes. We played together for quite a while. And uh yeah on your earliest job about 1924 in Niles which is a northern suburb of Chicago you thought you might have run into Shields. At any rate it was the New Orleans clarinetist who taught you to play
eccentric. That's right we learned eccentric uh eccentric rag and I believe it was Larry Shields
that taught us. Yeah at any rate you do remember that Rag Baby Stevens played it. Oh yes. In Athens uh

We used to come and play quite regular with us. It was called House of Niles. House of Niles. I think they played picnics out in through there and they would stop in for a beer afterwards and set in with the band. Oh yeah. I don't know how we could have earned eccentric any other way and we learned it. And uh I think I think Larry Shields taught us. I can't be sure. I think Leon Rapolo came uh came back to Chicago when I was playing with Ray Bozeman and uh played one night but it's been so long I can't remember. I'm pretty

sure that I met him though. Uh Merez and uh Brunas for a long time held a job at Friars Inn, one of the best loop jobs in Chicago. And uh you were in a succeeding band weren't you? Yes. Paley's band. Bill Paley's band uh and you were the trumpet player along with uh uh Caffarelli was
he the other? Gene Caffarelli yes. Yeah. And uh you thought by that time Steve Brown was out of
the place though and you probably encountered Steve Brown where? At Midway Gardens where I played
at Midway Gardens at succeeding times and at one of the times I believe Steve was there. Uh
He may have been. Probably he was the leader. Elmer was the leader one of the times I believe Floyd

Town another. I played also with Elmer at Guy in Paradise Ballroom and uh with Charmie Strait at times uh when Beiderbeck wasn't playing with him and uh during the during the middle 20s. Several people
have remarked about a resemblance between your tone and perhaps your style and Natty Dominick's and

how do you suppose that developed? From listening to him I think and liking the way he played more than anything else. He said he's writing that was about as nice a way to play as any and it just was a style
that seemed to develop naturally with me. Unfortunately we couldn't get Natty up here tonight we hope that uh
I tried to talk him into it but he was he was he was a little sore because the Giants lost the series
he didn't want to come. Well I'm sorry too that Natty has decided he's going to give up uh Trumpet at 70.

I suppose it's not a difficult decision. I promised him I'd go out to his house and take my horn tomorrow or next afternoon one of the afternoons before I leave Chicago and I intend to do that if I can

and uh have some fun with it. There haven't been many examples of the uh fellas from the north side who actually formally studied under those on the south side but you mentioned some today you mentioned that Fortin a piano player uh studied under uh Teddy Weatherford. Yes he did. Uh do you remember that Johnny Lane took some lessons from uh Jimmy Noon I believe? He may have and he uh he either

studied directly with uh Johnny Dodge. Incidentally I played uh some jobs with uh Johnny's brother Baby Dodge quite a few jobs before I left the music business. He may have studied directly with Johnny uh Johnny Lane may have or uh copied his records I don't know which. Now Davey Rose uh may have taken personal lessons from Earl Hines I don't know. I know that he listened to him at the apex later called the nest. Well there were many. He may have taken personal lessons from him in his house. I wouldn't be
surprised if he did. Possibly. There were many who uh they were very close friends. They studied his style and his records and visited with him. You told me that you visited out Apex on occasion.

Well I used to go there regularly two or three times a week and Earl had a little box that I would sit on behind the piano keyboard with him and it was regularly sort of my place to sit and I'd always sit there with him and there was many times and Jimmy was playing the clarinet Jimmy Noonie and Zutty was playing the drums. I don't remember Zutty Singleton. I don't remember the saxophone player's name any longer. Zutty wasn't drummer regularly with
that group now. You're quite sure they were here at the time at the time. Yes he was there. Uh there was

another drummer. I can't remember his name. Uh I used to meet Earl and uh Louie Armstrong after they finished work and we would just bum around a little bit together. Chatted up a bit here and there. That was back when Louie was playing at the uh Sunset and later at the Grand Terrace. Uh Earl was at the Grand Terrace and Louie was at the Regal I believe. I think Carol Dickerson went to the Regal. Uh well Savoy I mean the Savoy Ballroom. Savoy Ballroom. And we used to hear Clarence Williams play at the Vendome Theater occasionally too. He used to bring a band in his Vendome. And sometimes into the Savoy Ballroom. Uh-huh. Bunk Johnson I knew him when he came back to uh Chicago in 1945 and 46 with Don Ewell. Don was a house guest off and on a little bit and uh I played a little with Bunk. Not much but some. Not as much as

I'd like to have. You said the spot on North Broadway. Someplace around. In Argyle. That would make it a place that he played for a few nights. Yes. With uh Darnell Howard and I think Ewell and and you encountered them there. You were in. Yes I was asked to go there one night with my horn. I went
and I played a little with him. I can't remember who invited me any longer. Well when Bunk came it was

quite a revelation that there was still some this uh uh early uh uh New Orleans style still around and and uh it was easy to recognize the quality of the world. I played a jazz concert about that time at

the Moose Hall. It was after I came out of the army and I don't remember if Bunk was there that day or not. He may have been. I know Baby Dot was there and we played together that day. Uh Bud Freeman was there. Tut's Oper. Well I can't remember who all was there. What year did that mean? Uh 1945 or 46. It was supposed to be a jazz concert for me but it was all mixed up. We we shared honors equally pretty much. I have a vague recollection of being a participant in a jazz concert during the war years. It was probably 19 I was I was home in uniform and it was at Orchestra Hall and I think there were two of them on successive Sundays and I was there both times. I played a little I think. I can't remember it. It's been so long ago but Catherine Jacobson could tell you all about it. I think she sponsored the things and they were very well attended. The recollection is very vague. I think Fats Waller was there. Pretty sure. I know that the Burt Kelly Stables Band was there and it seems to me that I played a set with the Stables Band and played some Natty Dominic that day. Oh. But it uh it's begging my mind. Catherine Jacobson could fill you in on the whole thing if you can reach her. Get in touch with her. She's in Florida. I think.

John uh during the time I was talking before when I was here about the musicians I'd known that came from New Orleans. I forgot to mention several. Uh one of them was Wingy Minoni. I knew him of course through the years he was in Chicago during the 20s and 30s. Matter of fact I roomed with him for a while on Lawrence Avenue and uh that was a time when Wingy was quite depressed. He was uh worried about his mother who was I believe in New Orleans or someplace in Louisiana and she was ill at the time and he was quite worried about her. And there was Jack Locano, a trombone player. Do you remember where Wingy was working working in these days? He wasn't working much right then. Uh was it a hotel? No it was a rooming house. We moved we moved there. I forget what year it was. Is this the place that Art Hody speaks about? Was Art in later with Wingy? Wingy uh Wingy and Art may have stayed there. I moved away and Art may have moved in. I moved away and uh I was married at that time and I was married off and on. It was an off and on kind of marriage and I think I went back with my wife then and uh Hody's may have
moved in. Did you mention that Wingy had a rehearsal band? Well he had several rehearsal bands. One of them

I was in and I think Max Kaminsky was the other trumpet in it. I think Marty Marcel was the other trumpet at one time. Floyd O'Brien was in it. Uh I think uh uh most everybody was in it that was around and once in a while we'd play a job sometimes we wouldn't. Wingy had uh a job in that ballroom at uh Sheffield and uh Belmont. Uh did he have that job in this period? About that time. Yeah. But I wasn't in the band. I don't think I may have been. Come to think of it I did play there or some play. I played in some ballroom with him a little bit. It wasn't much of a job. I think it was two or three nights a week and it lasted a little while. And Wingy was in front of the band and he would he would play a chorus now and then and sing. There was Jack Loicano uh uh and he had a brother Deacon Loicano. They called him Deacon. Uh Jack played trombone and uh Deacon played string bass. And I played with both of them a great deal. This was mainly a jobbing uh Jobbing mainly. Sometime I think I played a steady job or two with the Deacon Loicano. One of the chop suey places probably. Might have been Cinderella. Cinderella Ballroom I know I played did play with him. That was a 10 or 11 piece band. Would you be able to guess the date? 1926 to 28 and through there. 27 probably. 1927. I think Bernard Dixon was in the, Dick Dixon was in the band. But where, what was the location of Cinderella? It was on uh around 63rd and Cottage. It was right across the street about a block from the trianon. And they uh they always had a band of eight to 10 or 11 pieces there. I played there with I believe three different leaders three different times. And that was when I was playing at the trianon and then at the little uh chop suey place at the corner of 63rd and uh 63rd and Cottage. I played there sometimes too. Sterling Bowes used to come there. And uh this saxophone player I was trying to mention uh the other night was Larry Tice. He used to come there and set in with us regular in this little place at 63rd and Cottage at the corner. He knew Bix by the way. He knew him quite well. Larry did. Yes certainly. He wanted me to go with him one night to uh see Bix and for some reason I didn't go. I don't know why it was. That was in the later, that was not too long before Bix went to New York and uh was killed or died. That's right it was Rod that fell down wasn't it? Bix died of lower pneumonia. But I remember that time Larry came by for me. It was raining or something and uh I didn't go with him. I should have. I used to go to the trianon and hear uh little Sterling play. He played very well. Is he still alive? Do you know? No. That was Jules Cassard. He used to play string bass mostly but two but some and I played with him quite a bit. I can't remember just where. Columbia Ballroom I think and other places. Jules Bufano, he's now with uh as far as I know with uh Jimmy Durante. I played a great deal with him with the Benson organization and uh we had a band together for a while. He was a very good bass player. He is still. Sandals Pecora, trombone. I played with him some good trombone player. There are others. I just can't remember them now. A lot of them I mentioned the other night. But these are some that I had forgotten and I thought that you ought to know about. I have to mention John that during the days that the Arcadia Ballroom was open I used to play with Husker Harris Orchestra there and I played opposite uh Elgar's orchestra quite a bit. We were a regular feature there. That would be in 1925, 26, 27 and 28 and through there and I think I played opposite Cook there later or earlier. I've forgotten which. There are also some color musicians that used to have a second band at the Midway. After Muggsy left there I went there with Mel Stitzel and then again with Floyd Towne.
